cells.tense: Right now you're the one finding the shape in things that aren't settled yet, and you're doing it without needing the whole answer first.
cells.ask: Tell one person what you feel about a move you've already reasoned out — not whether you're right, just what it stirs in you. Their read of the room is something logic alone can't hand you.
cells.core:
You can hold a picture that's still mostly blank and take the next step anyway. The pattern shows up early for you — you see where something's heading before there's proof — and you carry that lightly, without turning it into a forecast that has to be defended. That's what makes you easy to move with when the road isn't clear.

The part that's untested here is how it lands on other people. You can read a situation cold and be accurate, and still miss what it's like to be inside it with someone. Letting their take in doesn't weaken yours; it gives you something your own head can't generate.
cells.sheetLine: You see the shape of things early, and you don't need the whole road to take the step.

cells.tense: You're running the analysis out ahead of where anyone could actually walk, bracing against an answer you haven't gotten yet.
cells.ask: Write your next sentence into the situation — one thing you'll actually say — and stop there. Leave the reply unwritten. That's enough to move from the exercise back into the room.
cells.core:
The raw skill is real — you can take apart a problem that hasn't fully formed and find the thread. That's the same mind that's useful when you're in the middle of something genuinely unclear and need to see what most people miss.

What's happening right now is that the working-out has replaced the work. You keep building the case, refining the read, testing the version that might finally hold — and the exercise has taken over the place where the actual step would go. The next move isn't more clarity; it's one utterance you can't take back, which is the only thing that will tell you what's true.
cells.sheetLine: You've been mapping the answer instead of making the move.

cells.tense: You're standing on the near side of a decision you've already half-made, still calling it too soon.
cells.ask: Say out loud to one person the direction you're actually leaning. Let their response meet what you've been carrying alone, without merging into it.
cells.core:
You have a real ability to feel your way through fog — to sense which way the path is bending before it's visible. That instinct is the thing that gets people unstuck, including you, when you let it lead. In a conversation that's going well, you notice the small opening forming and you move before it closes; you don't wait for permission from certainty. The ground stays soft under you and you keep walking.

What's slowed down is the act of saying what you already sense. The read has gone quiet in the open, and you've been treating that silence as if it meant nothing were there. It's there. What's missing is the moment it crosses from private to spoken — the only place it can actually move you.
cells.sheetLine: The read is still there. You've stopped letting it speak.

cells.tense: You're steering by a pattern you've already spotted, but you're describing it as if the terrain were doing the deciding.
cells.ask: Name one choice you've been calling someone else's call — say the words 'this one is mine' — and let it land once. That's the read holding its ground.
cells.core:
You're already navigating the unclear ground, and you're doing it well — picking the way forward before the picture is finished, adjusting as you go. In a good stretch, that shows up as calm in a room full of question marks; you move, and the people around you move with you, because the read is steady even when the situation isn't.

What hasn't caught up is the credit. The instinct is working and you keep assigning it somewhere else — to circumstance, to timing, to whoever else was in the room. Seeing the move as yours doesn't make it reckless; it makes it something you can build on.
